an3.36:1.1: The three “messengers of the gods” here are a sick man, an old man, and a dead man. Buddhist traditions usually reckon the number as four, with the addition of a renunciate who inspires the spiritual path. This is the story told originally of Bodhisatta Vipassī ([dn14:1.31.1]()), and later of Gotama. Five are noted in [mn130](), with the addition of a baby and a punished man. At [mn83:4.6]() the messengers are grey hairs. | In the Vedic tradition, the original messenger was Agni, the visible presence of divinity among humanity, brought from the fiery sun down to earth in the lightning (eg. Rig Veda 1.58.1, 3.54.19, 4.7.4, 5.26.6, 10.98.2). Other divinities might play a similar role, such as the wind (Atharva Veda 4.13.3). Later literature envisaged literal messengers sent to convey important information. As to the current context, see note below on the messengers of Yama.
an3.36:1.4: The ideas in this discourse are treated in more detail in [mn129]() and [mn130]().
an3.36:1.5: Yama is guardian to the paths or rivers that lead one from one life to another ([sn1.33:10.3](), [mn130:3.1](), [dhp235]()). As the son of Vivasvant (the sun) and Tvaṣṭar’s missing daughter Saraṇyū (Rig Veda 10.17.1–2), he was born immortal (1.83.5), but yielding to the seduction of his sister Yamī, albeit reluctantly (10.10, 10.12.6), he chose mortality “for the sake of the gods and offspring” (10.13.4). As the first person to die, he discovered the paths to the lands of the dead that he now guards with his pair of hounds (10.14). Yama is a righteous god, but sinners see him as horrifying due to their own guilt (Brahma Purāṇa 106.46). The Zend Avesta depicts him as the righteous ruler of an abundant land to the north, from which the ancestors spread south. This very old tradition suggests his original legend was king of the ancient Proto-Indo-European people, thus quite literally “king of the land of the fathers”, who discovered the paths south, which now lead back to the lands of the fathers. The Indians, vaguely recalling an idealized home in the far north, called it Uttarakuru ([dn32:7.1]()). | As to why a twin guards the pathways of the dead, these passages abound in dyads, such as the “twin” carts that bring soma to the ritual, or the two destinies of the dead, the gods or the forefathers. I think the critical motif of consensual incest with a twin, though hard to speak of (10.12.6), emphasizes the merging of the self in the act of sex, the loss of individual identity binding oneself to death through the creation of offspring. The inverse is the splitting of the self into two, the living body and the dead shade, which is desired as promising immortality and feared as the reminder of mortality. These dual anxieties cling to the cremation fire, which is urged to not harm the dead, then immediately to cook them and send them to the ancestors (10.16.1), “who have Yama as king” (10.16.9). In this way Yama is bound to Agni, the original messenger of the gods. This is of more than incidental significance for the history of Vedic, and hence Buddhist, thought, for in the call for a dying man to “unite with Yama in the highest heaven” (10.14.8) we discern a precedent to the Upaniṣadic idea of the temporary separation of the self from divinity, or its forgetting of its true nature as divinity, and the eternal return.
an3.36:1.6: Where Yamī speaks of desire and transgression, Yama takes the part of old tradition and the laws of the just gods, for “lofty is the ordinance of Mitra and Varuṇa” (Rig Veda 10.10.6).
an3.36:1.7: As a king punishes a criminal ([mn129:8.3](), [sn12.70:28.3]()). Nonetheless, Yama does not, in fact, impose punishment ([an3.36:5.3]()). For more on the “wardens of hell” see note on [mn129:10.1]().
an3.36:2.1: The original messenger of Yama was no benign sign of mortality, but the two hounds of the underworld, descendants of Indra’s dog Saramā, “stealers of lives” who, with their “eyes on men”, “pursue the peoples” (Rig Veda 10.14.10–12). Tradition names them Śyāma (“Brownie”) and Śabala (“Spot”), which we find at [snp3.10:27.2]() in a description of the hounds of hell. They find a counterpart in the horrifying Kaṇha, the “black hound” sent by Sakka to terrify humanity into good behavior ([ja469]()).
an3.36:2.4: The truth is all around us, yet we proceed as if it was hidden.
an3.36:5.3: It is not Yama who punishes, but the wardens of hell.
an3.36:5.5: Yama teaches the Buddhist doctrine of personal responsibility for deeds. The gods can merely warn us, not save us from our deeds.
an3.36:10.4: These days, we hide old people in nursing homes, sick people in hospitals, and dead bodies in funeral homes, while filling our media with beautiful, able-bodied young people enhanced surgically and digitally. Our entire culture is devoted to not seeing the divine messengers.
an3.36:13.1: Yama does not judge or condemn, he holds a mirror up to a person’s life and calls them to account. It is up to each person to acknowledge what they did. This follows the same principle as the monastic Vinaya, where in almost every case it is required that an individual confess and acknowledge what they did before any procedure can be carried out. | The following passage is also found at [mn129:10.1]().
an3.36:13.2: The history of hell in India begins with the Rig Veda, which speaks of evildoers facing the “erasure of the wolf”, the “downfall” (2.29.6c), the “bottomless darkness” (7.104.3) “beneath all three earths” (7.104.11), the “endless abyss” (7.104.17), the “darkness below” (10.152.4). Atharva Veda similarly speaks of the “house below” (2.14.3a), the “deepest dark” (8.2.24). It also consigns a man stingy with cattle to the _nārakaṁ lokaṁ_, which seems to mean “the world of the hell beings” (12.4.36c); there is an equally vague reference to a “hell being” at Śukla Yajur Veda 30.5. These seem to be the earliest uses of the word _naraka_ in the sense of “hell”; this sense is not found in early Pali (see note on [dn12:78.2]()). Jaiminīya Brāhmaņa 1.42 describes the “other world” in both hellish and heavenly terms (see too Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 11.6.1). It depicts the hellish torments taking place in regions of the “other world” rather than as a distinct hell realm; and it does not share many details in common with later accounts. Thus far the texts are pre-Buddhist. It is not until the much later Purāṇic literature that lurid descriptions of hells, usually numbered 21 or 28, become a standard feature, along with the rest of the hell complex. Several of the places mentioned here correspond with the Purāṇic hells.
an3.36:13.4: I give a few examples of similar descriptions in the Purāṇas (and the Jain Sūtrakṛtāṅga), without any attempt to be comprehensive. | The notion that one does not die despite the suffering is also found at Bhāgavata Purāṇa 5.26.28 and Sūtrakṛtāṅga 1.5.1.16. | The lifespan of one in hell is illustrated in the story of Kokālika ([sn6.10]() = [an10.89]()), which is repeated at [snp3.10]() with an expanded description of the hells that bears much in common with the present discourse.
an3.36:15.7: Identified by the commentary with Avīci hell; cf. the reference to Avīci with its four doors at [iti89:5.3]().
an3.36:15.8: Here the text appears to quote a saying.
an3.36:18.3: As noted above, Vedic tradition holds that Yama was born immortal but chose to become mortal. The reason, however, is quite different.
an3.36:18.5: This statement is found only in the Pali text, although Chinese texts are effectively similar, in that they all speak of the Buddha’s clairvoyance.
an3.36:19.2: _Māṇava_, which normally means “Vedic student”, is occasionally used in the poetic sense of _manussa_ (“humans”). Both words mean “descendant of the first man, Manu”. Yama was Manu’s brother, both sons of Saraṇyū.
an3.36:22.1: Read _khemappattā_ per Thai, Cambopdian, and PTS editions, and as found in the parallel at [mn130:30.15]().
